seoDescription: Learn the essential first steps for every frame loom weaving project. This guide covers the foundational techniques to start a woven wall hanging, from gathering the right tools to warping your loom with proper tension. Follow along to master creating a solid base using cardstock for a straight edge, executing a secure twining stitch to lock your warp threads in place, and weaving several rows of plain weave. This foundational knowledge ensures your weaving starts strong and straight, setting you up for success.

chapters.title: Weaving the Cardstock Spacer
chapters.description: Discover how to weave a piece of cardstock into the warp using plain weave to create a straight, stable foundation to build your weaving upon.

chapters.title: Securing the Base with a Twining Stitch
chapters.description: A detailed guide on starting your weft with an initial row of plain weave and then executing a twining stitch to securely lock the warp threads in place.

chapters.description: Learn how to build the foundation with rows of plain weave, including the crucial technique of creating an arch to prevent the weaving from narrowing.

chapters.title: Finishing the Foundation & Next Steps
chapters.description: This chapter shows how to finish the foundation of your weaving, tuck in the final weft tail, and introduces the next step of adding fringe.

summary:
## Getting Started: Tools & Materials
To begin a weaving project, you'll need the following items:
- **Plied Yarn**: For the main body of the weaving (the weft).
- **Tapestry Needle**: A large-eyed needle for weaving the yarn.
- **Frame Loom**: The structure that holds the weaving.
- **Cardstock**: A folded piece (about 2.5" wide) to create a straight bottom edge.
- **Non-stretch Warp String**: The vertical threads that form the structure of the weaving.
- **Weaving Comb**: For packing the weft rows down evenly.
- **Scissors**

## Warping the Loom
The **warp** is the series of vertical strings tensioned on the loom, acting as the canvas for your weaving.
1.  **Start the warp**: Tie an overhand knot to create a loop at the end of your warp string.
2.  **Mount the warp**: Decide on the width of your weaving and place the loop on a starting notch at the bottom of the loom.
3.  **Create a single warp**: Guide the string up to the corresponding top notch, loop it around, and bring it down to the next adjacent notch at the bottom. Continue this up-and-down pattern.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Warp Tension**: The warp should be **taut**, but not overly tight. It will naturally tighten as you weave. After warping, check for even tension across all strings and adjust by pulling on loose/tight adjacent strings to balance them out.

## Creating a Solid Foundation
Before weaving with yarn, a stable base is crucial for a straight final piece.

- **Cardstock Spacer**: Weave a folded piece of cardstock through the warp using a simple **plain weave** pattern (`over one, under one`). This provides a firm, straight edge to beat your first rows of yarn against.
- **Weft**: The **weft** refers to the horizontal yarn that you weave through the warp.

## Securing the Weaving with a Twining Stitch
The **twining stitch** is used to lock the warp strings in place, spacing them evenly and preventing them from shifting.

1.  **First Weft Row**: Weave one row of **plain weave**, leaving a long tail.
2.  **Create an Arch**: Gently push the weft into an arch before beating it down. This adds slack and prevents the sides from pulling inward.
3.  **Execute the Twine**: Working from one side to the other, wrap your weft yarn around every *other* warp string (specifically, the ones the first weft row goes *over*). Go down and under both the warp and the weft thread, then pull tight.
4.  **Beat Down**: Once the twining is complete, use your weaving comb to push the row down firmly against the cardstock.

## Building the Base with Plain Weave
To complete the foundation, add a few more rows of plain weave.

> [!TIP]
> **Preventing 'Draw-in'**: For every row of weft, always create a **subtle arch** before beating it down. This ensures there's enough yarn to travel over and under the warp without pulling the selvedge (side) warp threads inward. After making an arch, you can strum the warp strings to help settle the weft, then beat it down with your comb from the center outwards.
transcription:
## Introduction & Required Materials

Hey everyone, I'm Janelle, and if you've just discovered the wonderful craft of frame loom weaving and you're wondering how do I just get started on a weaving project, this video is for you. I'm going to show you exactly how I create the foundation for every woven wall hanging I make.

Before we get started, we'll quickly go through the tools and materials I'll be using to do this, and I will list and link them in the description box below as well. First up, we have some plied yarn, a tapestry needle, a frame loom, a folded over piece of cardstock that's about two and a half inches wide, a non-stretch warp string, a weaving comb, and a pair of scissors. That's everything that you're going to need to get started weaving.

## Warping the Loom

The first thing that we need to do is put a warp on the loom. The warp is kind of like a painter's canvas. So, this is the thing that's going to go onto the loom and stay there while we weave on top of it. So, we got to do that first.

Take your warp string, make a loop, and tie an overhand knot.

The next thing to do is to think about how big you want your weaving. So, that's kind of how wide. The length on this particular loom is fixed, so it's going to be the length that it is, but you can decide to warp only some of the loom or all of the loom. In this case, I'm going to start on the third groove on my loom. I'm going to take the warp string up to the third groove on the top as well, and then I'm just going to loop it around the notch. This is called a single warp. It's where we're just putting one warp string in between each notch.

So, I'm bringing it down, and I'm going to go to the next notch, and then I'm going to continue going up and down. As far as the tension goes, you don't need to ream on your warp string. You want it to be taut, as you can see here, but you don't want it to be super tight. The reason you don't want it to be super tight is because as you weave, the warp is naturally going to get a little bit tighter as you go.

I'm going to do one more so that I have 16 loops at the top. And now that we're at the bottom, there's a couple things I'm going to do. First, I'm just going to hold the warp string like this, and I'm going to just sort of run my hand along the warp, and just see if it feels even, you know, there's not any super loose or super tight warp strings. If there is, don't panic, that's okay. You might want to start over, but you don't have to. Starting over is great practice, and this is kind of one of those things that you need to get a feel for. Mine is feeling pretty even, so I'm happy with that.

## Tying Off and Adjusting Tension

I'm going to loop this string back around, leave myself a nice long tail, and then what I'm going to do is I'm holding the last warp string while I tie a knot. And I want to try to keep this as tight as I can while I do it. And I'm going to try tying a triple knot just for safety, and I'm paranoid.

Then I can cut off a little bit of the excess just so it's not in our way. So now I'm feeling this warp, this string feels a little bit loose. The way that you can tighten that back up... and then the one next to it feels a little bit tight. So I'm literally going to pull down on the string that's too loose, and then pull up on the one that's tight, and that's feeling a little more even.

All we're looking for when it comes to the evenness of your tension is just that we don't have some strings that are super tight and some strings that are super loose. So you're going to want to even those out if you have that.

## Weaving the Cardstock Spacer

The next thing that we're going to do now that the warp is on and we're happy with the tension is we're going to weave in our cardstock. The thing I like about doing this method is that you have something that is sturdy and straight to beat down onto as you're weaving so that the bottom of your weaving doesn't go crooked on you.

We're going to weave this in with plain weave. And plain weave or tabby is just the most basic form of weaving. It's simply just over one warp string, under one warp string, over, under, over, under. And then we can just sort of push this down to the very bottom of our looms.

## Securing the Base with a Twining Stitch

Next, we're going to take the plied yarn, and we're going to create the base, the foundation for this piece. We're going to be doing a twining stitch first, and then some plain weave. So, what I'm going to do is I'm going to get about five widths of my loom worth of yarn, plus just a little bit more. And then I'm going to take my tapestry needle and thread that.

Now, we're going to start putting in what is called our weft. So, the weft is just the horizontal strings that go in and through the warp. We're starting with plain weave, and since our cardstock ended on an under this warp string, we're going to go the opposite and go over that. So, we're simply again going over, under, over, under all the way across our loom, and we're going to leave a nice long tail here, so that can be tucked in later.

Now, I'm just going to create a little arch with my weft. This is so that it doesn't get too tight, and then I'm going to just simply push it closer to the cardstock. It doesn't need to touch it, though. Now, we're ready to do our twining stitch. So, with a twining stitch, everywhere that the weft is going over top of the warp, we're going to be working on those strings. So, the weft is going over the warp string. I'm pointing my needle down. We're working from left to right. So, I'm pointing it down, and I'm going down and under and through like this.

So, we're going to pull that all the way through. We're going to tighten it up a bit, including with this end. And we're going to do that again. So, I'm tossing my yarn over here. And then I'm going with the weft string going over the warp again. So, we're skipping this warp string. We're going to the next one, and we're going underneath both the warp and the weft, and then through like this. Then we're going to tighten that up. And do the same thing again. So, the weft is going over the warp on this one. We're going down, under, and through like this. And then pulling it tight.

And we'll do one more together. So, we're skipping the next warp string, and then we're going underneath that one and through. And that can be continued all the way across. And as you're doing this, you just want to make sure that you keep on tightening it up. We don't want to pull in the sides of the warp strings. We just want everything to be tight on the warp strings. Then I'm taking my comb, and now that I'm done, you know, this section, I can kind of push it down more firmly onto the cardstock.

On the very last warp string, because the weft is going over top of it, we are going to go underneath that as well. And again, just tighten that up. And what this does is it secures our warp. This is going to be super helpful for when you're taking your weaving off of your loom. It's not going to allow things to slide around as much. And it also, as you can see, makes our warp strings really nice and even. So, we can make sure that's all now pushed nice and firmly down onto the cardstock.

## Weaving the Foundation with Plain Weave

And now we're ready for a couple rows of plain weave. I like to do three total rows in addition to the twining stitch. So, our weft ended underneath this warp string. So, now we need to start going over and we're going to just go over under over under all the way across.

Then what we're going to do is we're pulling this firmly against our warp string. I like to sort of pinch it so I don't pull it in like this. So, I'm pulling it out like this. Then I'm going to create an arch. The reason we need to do this is that if we don't create an arch and make sure that there's enough slack in our weaving, it's actually going to make your warp string start coming in and in and in as you go. After you make your arch, you can give your warp a little bit of a strum. And then you're going to take your weaving comb. I like to push it down in the middle and then go to the sides and push it down there as well.

And now we're going to repeat that same process. So, on this end we ended with our weft coming under the warp. So, now we need to start going over that warp string. And we're going over under all the way across. So, once again, I'm pulling my weft taut against the warp string here on the left, but I'm still holding it so that I'm not sucking it too far in.

I'm creating an arch. Give your warp a strum. Beat it down in the middle and then off to the sides. And something I like to do if I do feel like I'm pulling the warp strings in all on the sides is I'll simply just start, you know, pinching it a little bit and pulling it back out as I go.

## Finishing the Foundation & Next Steps

So, now that we're finished the base of our weaving and then we're ready to do the fringe, we can cut off a little bit of a tail. Since this is all going to be hidden under fringe, I'm going to take that little end and just weave it in a few strings and then just tuck it behind my loom to be tucked in later when I'm done weaving.

Now that you have a foundation for your piece, you're ready for fringe. So, check out this video next for how to attach fringe to your weaving.
